guide_line: Count the valence electrons, join the atoms with pairs, and give each atom an octet except hydrogen.
steps: Add the valence electrons. For main-group atoms, that count is the group number of valence electrons. A negative charge adds electrons. A positive charge removes electrons.
The central atom is usually the atom that is not hydrogen and is less electronegative.
Draw a single bond to each outside atom. Each bond uses two electrons.
Place leftover electrons on the outside atoms first, in pairs, until each outside atom has an octet. Hydrogen only needs two electrons.
If the central atom is still short of eight, move a lone pair from an outside atom into a double or triple bond.
Three common exceptions: an odd-electron molecule such as NO, an electron-deficient center such as boron in BF3, and an expanded octet on a period-3-or-higher center such as sulfur in SF6.

worked_example.q: How many valence electrons are in H2O, and how many lone pairs sit on oxygen?
steps: Oxygen has 6 valence electrons and each hydrogen has 1. The total is 8.
The other 4 electrons stay on oxygen as two lone pairs.

similar_problem.q: How many valence electrons are in NH4+?
similar_problem.hint: Start with nitrogen’s 5 valence electrons and one from each hydrogen. A 1+ charge means you remove one electron from that sum.

problems.q: How many valence electrons are in NH4+?
problems.why: Nitrogen contributes 5 and four hydrogens contribute 4, for 9. The 1+ charge removes 1 electron. NH4+ has 8 valence electrons.
hints: Start with nitrogen’s 5 valence electrons and one from each hydrogen. A 1+ charge means you remove one electron from that sum.

problems.q: How many valence electrons are in CO3 2−?
problems.why: Carbon contributes 4 and three oxygens contribute 18, for 22. The 2− charge adds 2 electrons. CO3 2− has 24 valence electrons.
hints: Carbon brings 4 and each of the three oxygens brings 6. The 2− charge adds two more electrons.

problems.q: How many valence electrons are in NO3−?
problems.why: Nitrogen contributes 5 and three oxygens contribute 18, for 23. The 1− charge adds 1 electron. NO3− has 24 valence electrons.
hints: Add nitrogen’s 5 to 6 from each of three oxygens, then add the extra electron from the 1− charge.

problems.q: How many valence electrons are in PCl5?
problems.why: Phosphorus contributes 5. Five chlorine atoms contribute 5 × 7 = 35. The total is 40 valence electrons.
hints: Phosphorus contributes 5. Multiply chlorine’s 7 valence electrons by five and add those two contributions.

problems.q: How many valence electrons are in NO?
problems.why: Nitrogen contributes 5 and oxygen contributes 6. The total is 11, an odd number, so NO is a radical with one unpaired electron.
hints: Add the valence electrons of one nitrogen and one oxygen. Do not round the total to an even number.

problems.q: Which atom is central in CO2? Write the element symbol.
problems.why: Carbon is less electronegative than oxygen, and there is no hydrogen. Carbon is the central atom in CO2.
hints: Between carbon and oxygen, put the less electronegative atom in the middle.

problems.q: Which atom is central in HCN? Write the element symbol.
problems.why: Hydrogen is always an outside atom. Carbon is less electronegative than nitrogen, so the skeleton is H–C–N. Carbon is central.
hints: Hydrogen cannot be the center. Of the two atoms that remain, choose the one with the lower electronegativity.

problems.q: How many lone pairs are on the oxygen atom in H2O?
problems.why: Oxygen has 6 valence electrons. Two are used in the O–H bonds. The remaining 4 electrons are two lone pairs.
hints: Oxygen starts with 6 valence electrons. Subtract the two electrons it uses for the two O–H bonds, then group what remains into pairs.

problems.q: How many shared electron pairs are there between the two nitrogen atoms in N2?
problems.why: Each nitrogen has 5 valence electrons and needs 3 more for an octet. The two atoms share three pairs, which is a triple bond.
hints: Each nitrogen atom still needs three electrons after its own lone pair is placed. Those missing electrons are shared.

problems.q: In BF3, does the boron atom have a full octet? Answer yes or no.
problems.why: Boron has 3 valence electrons and forms three bonds. That is only 6 electrons around boron. BF3 is electron-deficient, so the answer is no.
hints: Count only the electrons touching boron. Three bonds supply six electrons, which is short of eight.

problems.q: How many lone pairs are on the sulfur atom in SF6?
problems.why: Sulfur has 6 valence electrons, and all six are used to make six S–F bonds. No electrons are left as a lone pair on sulfur.
hints: Sulfur has six valence electrons and six fluorines to bond. None of those electrons are left over on sulfur.

problems.q: How many valence electrons are in SF6?
problems.why: Sulfur contributes 6 and six fluorine atoms contribute 6 × 7 = 42. The total is 48 valence electrons.
hints: Sulfur contributes 6. Six fluorine atoms contribute 7 each. Add those two groups.

problems.q: In the best Lewis structure of CO2, how many double bonds does carbon form?
problems.why: Two single bonds leave carbon with only 4 electrons. Making both C–O links double bonds gives carbon an octet. CO2 has two double bonds.
hints: Two single bonds leave carbon short of eight electrons. Complete the octet by raising both C–O links.

problems.q: Can the sulfur atom in SF6 hold more than 8 electrons? Answer yes or no.
problems.why: Sulfur is in period 3, so it can expand its octet. In SF6 the sulfur atom is surrounded by 12 electrons. The answer is yes.
hints: Check sulfur’s period. Atoms in period 3 and below can be surrounded by more than eight electrons.
